title: Doubles and precision
objectives: Compare doubles safely and avoid catastrophic cancellation.

screens.title: The same 0.3
screens.prose:
In Python, `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` was `False`. Here is the same test in C++.

```cpp
std::cout << (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) << '\n';
```

Each dot is a double near 0.3, counted in gaps from the double closest to 0.3.
screens.question: What does the line print?

options.why: You added on paper. Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 is stored exactly, and their rounded sum lands one double above 0.3.
The comparison is false, but `std::cout` prints a `bool` as 0 or 1 unless you send it `std::boolalpha` first.

options.text: Nothing: `==` on doubles does not compile
options.why: It compiles silently. Only the opt-in warning `-Wfloat-equal` mentions it.

hints.text: C++ stores 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 as the same 64-bit doubles Python uses.
The sum lands on one of the other dots.
The test is false, and `std::cout` prints `false` as 0.

feedback.correct: The test is false, printed as 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out whether the test is true, then how `std::cout` prints a `bool`.

byKey.one: You added on paper. The rounded sum lands one double above 0.3, so `==` is false.
byKey.false: `std::cout` prints a `bool` as 0 or 1 unless you send it `std::boolalpha`.

explain.text: 0.1 and 0.2 are each stored a little off, and their sum rounds to the double one gap above 0.3. So `==` is false and `std::cout` prints 0. C++ and Python share the same doubles, so every float fact you know carries over.

screens.title: Inside a double
screens.prose: A `double` is 64 bits in three boxes. Box 2 shows its first 12 bits of 52. Slide through the values and watch which boxes change.
screens.question: Drag each name onto the box it describes.

hints.text: Slide from 1 to 2 to 4: each value doubles. Which box changes?
Value 4 is −2. Compare it with value 1, which is 2.
Doubling changes box 1 only. The minus sign flips box 0 only. Going from 2 to 3 changes box 2 only.

feedback.correct: Box 0 is the sign, box 1 the exponent, box 2 the mantissa.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide through the values and see which box each change touches.

byKey.sign: Slide to −2: only box 0 differs from 2, so box 0 holds the sign.
byKey.exponent: Slide 1, 2, 4: each doubling adds 1 to box 1 and leaves box 2 alone. Box 1 is the power of 2.
byKey.mantissa: Slide from 2 to 3: only box 2 changes, because 3 is 1.5 × 2. Box 2 holds the digits.

explain.text: The value is $(-1)^{s} \times 1.m \times 2^{e - 1023}$: sign $s$, exponent $e$, mantissa $m$. 0.1 is $1.6 \times 2^{-4}$, and 1.6 has no finite binary form, so its 52 bits are cut short. The exponent sets the scale; the 52 mantissa bits set the precision.

screens.title: The next double after 1
screens.prose: 1.0 has a mantissa of 52 zeros. The next double up sets only the last of those 52 bits to 1. Each place in the mantissa is worth half the one before it.

state.caption: The doubles just above 1, one gap apart

screens.question: How far above 1 is the next double, in units of $10^{-16}$?

hints.text: The first mantissa bit is worth $\tfrac12$, the second $\tfrac14$.
The 52nd bit is worth $2^{-52}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what the 52nd mantissa bit is worth.

byKey.half: That is $2^{-53}$, one place too far. The mantissa has 52 bits, so its last bit is worth $2^{-52}$.
byKey.sixtyfour: That is $2^{-64}$. The sign and exponent use 12 of the 64 bits, so the mantissa has 52.
byKey.decimal: Doubles are binary, so the gap is a power of 2, not of 10: $2^{-52}$.

explain.text: The last mantissa bit is worth $2^{-52} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}$ at 1. C++ names it `std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()`, from `<limits>`, and `std::nextafter(1.0, 2.0)` returns that next double. So a double holds about 16 significant digits.

screens.title: Gaps near 10¹⁶
screens.question: What does the code print?

hints.text: Is $10^{16} + 1$ one of the dots?
$10^{16} + 1$ sits exactly halfway between two dots.
A tie rounds to the neighbour whose last mantissa bit is 0, which here is $10^{16}$ itself. Then $10^{16} - 10^{16} = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round $10^{16} + 1$ to a dot first, then subtract.

byKey.exact: You added exactly. Near $10^{16}$ the doubles are 2 apart, so $10^{16} + 1$ has no double of its own.
byKey.up: $10^{16} + 1$ is a tie between $10^{16}$ and $10^{16} + 2$. Ties round to the even mantissa, which here is $10^{16}$.

explain.text: $10^{16} + 1$ is halfway between two doubles, and the tie rounds back to $10^{16}$. A double keeps about 16 significant digits at every size, and near $10^{16}$ none is left for the units. The gap is always about $2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ times the number itself.

screens.title: A tolerance of 1e-9
screens.question: What does `same(a, b)` return, and is the book broken?

options.text: `false`, but nothing is wrong: the totals are neighbouring doubles
`true`: they differ by far less than a penny
options.why: You compared the difference with a penny. The code compares it with 1e-9, and 2.98e-8 is bigger.
A dropped position would move the total by pounds, not by 3e-8. The totals are one double apart.
`std::abs` only removes the sign. It rounds nothing.

hints.text: Compare 2.98e-8 with 1e-9.
The last row is the smallest difference two doubles near £250m can have.
No two different doubles near £250m are within 1e-9 of each other, so `same` is just `==`.

feedback.correct: The tolerance is smaller than the gap, so `same` acts like `==`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 2.98e-8 with the tolerance in the code.

byKey.penny: The code's tolerance is 1e-9, not a penny, and 2.98e-8 is larger. So `same` returns false.
byKey.dropped: The totals differ by one gap between doubles, not by a position. Rounding alone did this.

explain.text: Near £250m neighbouring doubles are $2^{-25} \approx 2.98 \times 10^{-8}$ apart. An absolute tolerance of 1e-9 is below that gap, so it is `==` in disguise and flags every rounding wobble. Scale the tolerance with the size of the numbers.

screens.title: A relative tolerance
screens.prose:
Scale the tolerance by the larger size, but never by less than 1, so values near zero still compare:

$$|a - b| \le \text{rel} \times \max(1, |a|, |b|).$$

`std::max` of three values takes a braced list: `std::max({x, y, z})`, from `<algorithm>`.
screens.question: Write `close(a, b, rel)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 9 hidden tests that call close; each must return exactly true or false.

hints.text: Compute `std::abs(a - b)` and compare it with `rel` times a scale.
Test 5 compares 0 with 1e-13. A purely relative tolerance shrinks to nothing at zero.
`double scale = std::max({1.0, std::abs(a), std::abs(b)});` then `return std::abs(a - b) <= rel * scale;`.

feedback.correct: Relative for big numbers, absolute near zero, and false for NaN.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3` are one gap apart, so `==` says no. Compare the difference with a tolerance.
byKey.test-5: Comparing 0 with 1e-13 failed. Without the 1.0 inside the max, the tolerance at zero is zero. Keep the floor of 1.
byKey.test-7: Two NaNs compared as close. If you wrote `!(diff > tol)`, that is true for NaN, because every comparison with NaN is false. Write `diff <= tol`.

explain.text: Away from zero, `rel` works as a number of significant digits: 1e-12 asks for about 12. Near zero the 1.0 in the max turns it into an absolute tolerance, which is what a comparison with 0 needs. A NaN makes `<=` false, so NaN is never close to anything, not even NaN.

screens.title: Digits that cancel
screens.prose: For small $x$, $1 - \cos x \approx x^2/2$. The table compares `1 - std::cos(x)` with the true value.
screens.question: How many significant digits of `1 - std::cos(1e-6)` are right?

hints.text: Line the two values up digit by digit.
5, 0, 0, 0 agree; the fifth digit is 4 against 0. That is 4 right digits.

feedback.correct: Four digits survive out of about 16.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the leading digits that agree in row 3.

byKey.all: A double holds about 16 digits, but the subtraction threw most away. Compare 5.00044... with 5.00000....
byKey.fifteen: A double holds about 16 digits, but the subtraction threw most away. Compare 5.00044... with 5.00000....
byKey.twelve: Twelve digits were lost, not kept. Compare 5.00044... with 5.00000....
byKey.five: The fifth digit is 4 in one and 0 in the other, so it is wrong. Four agree.

explain.text: $\cos(10^{-6}) = 0.9999999999995$, stored to about 16 digits. Subtracting it from 1 cancels the twelve leading 9s, leaving about 4 good digits. This is **catastrophic cancellation**: subtracting nearly equal numbers keeps their errors and loses their digits.

screens.title: Remove the subtraction
screens.prose:
The half-angle identity gives the same quantity with no subtraction:

$$1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2(x/2).$$

Write `stable_one_minus_cos(x)` with it.
screens.question: Write `stable_one_minus_cos(x)` with no cancellation.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests. Small answers are scaled up first, as in stable_one_minus_cos(1e-8) * 1e16, then accepted within a relative 1e-9.

hints.text: Compute $\sin(x/2)$ once and square it.
At $x = 10^{-8}$, `std::cos(x)` rounds to exactly 1, so any formula with `1 - std::cos` returns 0.
`double s = std::sin(x / 2); return 2 * s * s;`

feedback.correct: No subtraction, so no digits cancel.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: At 1e-8 you returned 0: `std::cos(1e-8)` rounds to exactly 1, so `1 - cos` is 0. Use the sine form.
byKey.test-3: At 1e-4 the answer is off in the ninth digit: the subtraction is still there. Use only the sine.

explain.text: `std::sin(x / 2)` is accurate to about 16 digits even for tiny $x$, and squaring and doubling keep them. The identity moved the cancellation into exact algebra on paper. Look for this rewrite whenever code subtracts two nearly equal values.

screens.title: A million 0.1s
screens.prose: Each addition rounds, and over a long sum the errors pile up. **Kahan summation** keeps the part each addition lost in `c` and adds it back on the next step. The starter's comments give the four steps.
screens.question: Write `kahan_sum(xs)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests that call kahan_sum; each sum must equal the expected double exactly.

hints.text: Replace `sum += x;` with the four commented steps.
`c` must live outside the loop, so each step can correct the next.
`double y = x - c; double t = sum + y; c = (t - sum) - y; sum = t;`

feedback.correct: Each lost part comes back in the next addition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: A million 0.1s should give exactly 100000. If you got 100000.00000133288, the loop still does a plain `sum += x`.
byKey.test-2: {1e16, 1, 1, −1e16} should sum to 2. A plain loop loses each 1 against 1e16; Kahan keeps it in `c`.

explain.text: `(t - sum) - y` is the rounding error of the last addition, and the next step subtracts it first. In `float`, with 24-bit mantissas, the plain sum is off by 1%, which is why pricing code uses `double`. Pairwise summation, adding in halves, is the other cure.

screens.title: Rules for doubles
screens.prose:
Everything on the earlier screens follows a few rules:

```cpp
close(a, b, 1e-12);    // never a == b
std::abs(pnl) < 0.005; // near 0: absolute
2 * s * s;             // not 1 - cos(x)
kahan_sum(xs);         // long sums
std::isnan(x);         // the NaN test
```
screens.question: Which test is true when `x` is NaN?

options.why: Every comparison with NaN is false, even with NaN itself.
NaN is not equal to itself, so this is false for NaN and true for every other value.
`std::abs(NaN)` is NaN, and NaN compared with anything is false.

hints.text: A comparison with NaN is always false.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every comparison involving NaN is false.

explain.text: NaN fails every `==`, `<` and `>`, so no comparison can find it. `std::isnan(x)` checks the bits directly, and `std::isfinite(x)` rules out infinity as well.

screens.title: A round trip that is not flat
screens.prose: You buy one share at each of £108.26, £103.47, £100.10 and £101.47. Then you sell them at the same prices, in reverse order. The P&L prints `-1.13687e-13`, and the end-of-day check flags any book where `pnl != 0.0`.
screens.question: Which check should the reconciliation use?

options.why: Against zero a relative tolerance is $10^{-9}$ times a tiny number, far below the error. Near zero you need an absolute tolerance.
1e-15 is below the rounding error of 1.1e-13, so the book still fails. The tolerance must sit above rounding noise and below a penny.
A `float` has fewer digits, so its rounding errors are larger, about 1e-5 here. The error does not go away.

hints.text: What is the smallest P&L that matters in money?
The check compares with zero, where relative tolerances shrink to nothing.
A penny matters; 1e-13 does not. Half a penny separates them.

feedback.correct: An absolute tolerance in money units, set below a penny.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each check with the error, 1.1e-13, and with a penny.

byKey.relative: You scaled the tolerance by `pnl` itself, which is tiny. Near zero only an absolute tolerance works.
byKey.tiny: 1e-15 is smaller than the error, so the flat book still fails.

explain.text: The two totals round differently, so a flat book shows −1.1e-13. Comparing with zero needs an absolute tolerance, and half a penny is the natural one. Many systems avoid the question by keeping prices in integer pence or ticks, as in the cpp course's *Every value has a type*: integers add exactly.

ideas: A double is a sign, an 11-bit exponent and a 52-bit mantissa: about 16 significant digits at any size.
Compare doubles with a relative tolerance and an absolute floor, never with `==`; near zero only an absolute tolerance works.
Subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits, and long sums pile up rounding: rewrite the formula, or carry the lost part as Kahan does.

formula.name: Safe comparison
formula.note: The 1 makes it absolute near zero; NaN is never close.

summary.trap: An absolute tolerance such as 1e-9 on a £250m value is smaller than the gap between doubles, so it acts like `==`.

options.why: You assumed a value always equals itself. `x` is NaN, and NaN equals nothing, not even NaN.
`<cmath>` does not stop the program on a bad input. It returns NaN.
The line prints the comparison, a `bool`, not `x`.

feedback.correct: NaN is not equal to itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `x` is NaN; what does `==` do with NaN?

explain.text: `std::sqrt(-1.0)` is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false, `x == x` included. Use `std::isnan(x)` to test for it.

quiz.prose:
A `float` has a 23-bit mantissa, so near 1.2 million its values are 0.125 apart.

```cpp
float notional = 1234567.89f;
```
quiz.question: What value does `notional` hold?

options.why: You assumed the literal is stored as written. A `float` keeps about 7 digits, so it rounds to the nearest multiple of 0.125.
Near 1.2 million a `float` still has 0.125 steps, so it keeps 1234567.875, not the next whole number.
Floats are binary: the nearest value is a multiple of 0.125, and 1234567.9 is not one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the multiple of 0.125 nearest 1234567.89.

explain.text: 1234567.89 lies between 1234567.875 and 1234568.0, and is nearer the first. A `float` loses a penny-level amount on a £1.2m notional, which is why pricing uses `double`.

quiz.prose: The gap between neighbouring doubles is about $2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ times the number.
quiz.question: Roughly how far apart are neighbouring doubles near £1,000,000?

options.why: That is the gap at 1. The gap grows with the number: multiply by a million.
That would leave only 12 significant digits. A double keeps about 16 at any size.
Doubles are binary and know nothing of pennies. The gap is a power of 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ by about a million.

explain.text: $10^6$ lies between $2^{19}$ and $2^{20}$, so the gap is $2^{19 - 52} = 2^{-33} \approx 1.16 \times 10^{-10}$. That is far finer than a penny, so `double` is plenty for prices of this size.

quiz.prose: You must add 1.0 and a million values of $10^{-16}$. The exact total is 1.0000000001.
quiz.question: Which order of adding gets close to the exact total?

options.text: Add the million small values first, then add 1.0
Start from 1.0 and add each small value to it
options.why: You started from 1.0. Each $10^{-16}$ is under half a gap at 1, so every addition rounds back to 1.0 and the total stays 1.

options.text: The order does not matter: addition is commutative
options.why: On paper, yes. In doubles each addition rounds, so the order changes the total.

options.text: Either order, if the values are `float`
options.why: A `float` has fewer digits, so the small values vanish even sooner.

feedback.correct: Small values first, so they can grow before meeting the big one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens to $1 + 10^{-16}$ in doubles?

explain.text: $1 + 10^{-16}$ rounds back to 1, so starting from 1.0 loses every small value. The small values summed together reach $10^{-10}$, which 1.0 can absorb. Kahan summation makes the order matter much less.
